scenes.headline: How Bun shrinks a compiled executable
scenes.sub: AOT compiles your code. Trim deletes the runtime you never call.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Wingnut! A Bun executable that prints one line is a hundred and forty megabytes. Here's how two new flags cut that down.

scenes.text: Compile your code to machine code at build time, then remove every Bun API the compiled program never calls.
scenes.say: The idea: compile your code ahead of time, so the compiler sees the whole program. Then delete every Bun API that program never calls.

steps.say: The compiler reads your code and every dependency, because ahead of time it must see the whole program.
While it does, it records which Bun and Node APIs are called by a name it can read.
Trim takes the full runtime and checks each API against that list.
Only the kept parts go into the executable. The rest is deleted.

scenes.title: Hello world, same program
scenes.say: Plain is one hundred forty megabytes. Trim alone gives eighty four. AOT alone gives sixty eight. Together, twenty five point six.

left.title: Written in source
left.say: If the source says Bun dot serve, the compiler sees the name and keeps the HTTP server.

right.title: Known at run time
right.say: If the name is only known at run time, trim removes it, and the call throws when it runs.

scenes.label: Startup of a Hono, zod and sqlite app
scenes.note: AOT is what helps launch time; trim does not
scenes.say: AOT also helps startup. A small app drops from thirty six to fourteen milliseconds. Trim saves bytes, not time.

scenes.text: Trim is only as good as the compiler's view of your program. Test the paths, not only the build.
scenes.say: Remember: trim trusts what the compiler can see. A clean build is not proof. Run the paths that matter.
AOT compiles ahead of time. Trim drops unused APIs. And a computed name can be removed.
